sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Arhat** ​(*arhat*) — ‌Worthy One, ‌Saint ​· an ​Arhat or ​superior ​divinity with ​the Jainas ‌— ​belongs to ​the Buddhist ‌tradition, ​where it ‌is catalogued ​under ‌the domain ​"Worthy One, ​Saint". ​The name ​means "an ​Arhat ‌or superior ​divinity ‌with the ​Jainas"[^1].

The ‌**arhat** ​is the ‌ideal of ​early ‌Buddhism made ​flesh: one ​who ‌has **destroyed ‌the taints, ‌done ​what had ​to be ‌done, ​and laid ​down the ‌burden** ​— freedom ​achieved in ‌this ​life, by ‌this person, ​without ​a god's ​intervention. The ​Theragāthā ‌lets the ‌finished saints ​speak ‌for themselves.[^2]

​PuniCodex records ​the ‌canonical scholarly ‌spelling **Arhat** ‌and ‌serves its ​temple at ‌[its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/arhat/). The ​displayed form ​is ‌ASCII-equivalent — ​a ​description computed ​from the ‌displayed ​form itself. ​The plain ​ASCII ‌form *arhat* ​contains the ‌same ​letters: no ‌recovered diacritics ​or ‌special encoding ‌is claimed. ​The ​work here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​Devanagari ​as ​**अर्हत्**. Etymologically ​it ​means ‌"an ​Arhat or ​superior ‌divinity ​with ‌the ​Jainas"[^1].

The ‌canonical ​spelling ​**Arhat** ​matches the ​conventional ​scholarly ‌romanization. ​The plain ‌ASCII ​form ‌*arhat* ​contains the ‌same ​letters, ‌so ​no lost ​diacritics ‌or ‌encoding ‌transition ​is claimed. ​The ‌editorial ​work ​is to ‌fix ​one ​reviewed ‌reference spelling, ​preserve ‌capitalization ​and ​provenance, and ​keep ​the ‌original ‌evidence visible. ​The ‌displayed ​form ​is ‌ASCII-equivalent — ‌a ‌description ‌computed ​from the ‌displayed ​form ​itself.

​The letter-by-letter ‌transformation ​runs:

- ​**a** ​→ **A** ‌— ​Same, ​capitalized
- ​**r** → ‌**r** ​— ‌Same
- ​**h** ‌→ **h** ​— ‌Same
- ‌**a** ​→ **a** ​— ​Same
- ​**t** ‌→ **t** ‌— ​Same

sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/arhat/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**arhat** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Arhat.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Arhat" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Arhat" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"arhat" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Arhat ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Arhat ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Arhat ‌place worthy ​one, ​saint ​at the ​center ​of a ‌living ​mythological world.

### ​Origins ‌(Myth)

​Arhat appears ‌in ​buddhist tradition ‌as ​worthy one, ​saint. ​The ​name's meaning, ​"an ‌Arhat or ​superior ‌divinity with ​the ‌Jainas", ​shapes the ‌narratives ​told about ‌this ​figure.

### Worship ​and ‌Memory ‌(Cult)

Devotees ‌and ​later tradition-keepers ​preserved ‌Arhat in ​ritual, ​text, ‌and iconography, ​ensuring ​the name ‌survived ​into the ‌modern ​scholarly record.

​The ​myths ​of Arhat ‌survive ‌in fragments, ​summaries, ‌and later ​retellings. ​Each ‌version reflects ‌the ‌interests of ‌its ​tellers — ‌poets, ​priests, ​philosophers, and ​scholars. ‌The PuniCodex ​entry ​does not ​privilege ‌a ​single version; ​it ​gathers the ‌attestations ​so that ‌readers ​can ‌compare them. ​The ‌restoration Arhat ‌gives ​the figure ​a ​stable ​name around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet assigned ​to ‌Arhat ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should be ​read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Buddhist ​name ‌of this ​type ‌the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected to ​be ​thin, ‌and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains the ‌textual ​testimony ​gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources section.

​Were ‌such ​evidence ​to ​surface, ​it ‌would take ‌recognizable ​forms: ‌votive ​or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming अर्हत्, ‌sanctuary ‌or ​cult ‌remains ​tied ​to worthy ​one ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional ​attributes (name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
The ​arhat is ‌the most ‌austere ideal ​any ​major religion ​has proposed: ​not love, ​not ‌justice, not ​obedience — ​**completion**. The ‌canonical ​formula is ‌brutal in ​its economy: ‌done ​is what ​had to ​be done; ​there ​is no ‌more of ​this. No ‌god ​approves it, ‌no history ​rewards it, ‌no ​heaven awaits ‌as payment. ​It is ​simply ‌over.

That ‌is why ‌the Mahāyāna ​found ​it both ‌admirable and ​insufficient, and ​why ‌modern readers ​find it ​quietly devastating. ‌The ​arhat does ‌not save ​the world; ​the ​arhat leaves. ​Yet the ‌tradition kept ‌the ​begging bowl ‌— the ​one object ​that ‌binds the ‌finished saint ‌back to ‌the ​unfinished crowd, ‌who must ​feed him ​and ​so plant ‌their own ​merit. Perfection, ​the ​bowl insists, ‌is not ​private. The ​worthy ​one stands ‌at the ​door precisely ‌so ​that someone ‌else can ​practice giving. ‌The ‌ideal of ​having nothing, ​it turns ​out, ​was always ‌also a ‌technology of ​**connection**.[^1]
